lesson.title: Right-triangle distances

lead.text: The two sides that meet at the right angle are the legs. The longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse.
Call the legs a and b and the hypotenuse c. Then a² + b² = c². A square root undoes squaring: the square root of 49 is 7, because 7 × 7 = 49.

steps.headline: In a right triangle, the squares of the two legs add to the square of the longest side.

lead.text: Use a² + b² = c². Square both legs and add them. That gives c², so a square root gives c.

reveal.text: You squared both legs, added, then took the square root. The straight side is shorter than the two legs added.

steps.headline: The legs are 3 m and 4 m. Find the hypotenuse, the shortcut.
A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find its hypotenuse.

lead.text: Check which sides are the legs before you square.

reveal.text: The same three moves as before: square, add, root.

lead.text: Sometimes the hypotenuse is given and a leg is missing. Start from a² + b² = c² and move a² to the other side.
The missing leg's square is c² minus the known leg's square. Then take the square root.

steps.headline: With the hypotenuse known, subtract to find a missing leg.

lead.text: This time the hypotenuse is known. Check which side it is before you subtract.

lesson.orientation: Find a missing side using squared lengths and identify when the Pythagorean theorem applies.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You walk 3 m east, then 4 m north. A friend says you could have cut straight across instead.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the longest side of a right triangle from the other two, and a missing leg from the longest.

recap.keyIdea: In a right triangle a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse. Add the squares of the legs, or subtract the known leg's square.

blocks.text: You found that the straight shortcut is shorter than the 7 m bent path, and that it comes to 5 m.
You also found a hypotenuse of 13 m from legs 5 m and 12 m, and a missing leg of 24 cm.

recap.nextHook: Right triangles also measure distances on a grid. Find out how.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs 5 m and 12 m. Find its hypotenuse in metres.
hints: Use the two sides meeting at the right angle.
Square and add the leg lengths.
Take the positive square root of 5² + 12².
questions.onCorrect: 13 m. Square the legs, add, then take the square root.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the legs. The theorem adds their squares, then takes the square root.
169 is the square of the hypotenuse. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: Which side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle?
hints: Find the right-angle corner. Which side is across from it?

acceptedIdeas: The side opposite the right angle
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The hypotenuse lies opposite the right angle, regardless of the triangle's orientation.

choices.label: The side opposite the right angle
Either side touching the right angle

questions.onCorrect: The hypotenuse faces the right angle. Turning the triangle does not change that.

misconceptions.feedback: The legs are the sides that touch the right angle. The hypotenuse is the third side.
Turning the triangle doesn't change which side faces the right angle.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find its hypotenuse in centimetres.
hints: The squares of the legs add to the square of the hypotenuse.
Find the sum of 6² and 8².
Take the positive square root of that sum.
questions.onCorrect: 10 cm. 36 + 64 = 100, and the square root of 100 is 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the legs. Adding the legs measures a bent path, not the straight side.
100 is the square of the hypotenuse. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: The hypotenuse is c and one leg is a. Which expression gives the other leg's length?
hints: Move a² to the other side of a² + b² = c².

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: From a² + b² = c², rearrange to b² = c² − a² and take the positive root.

questions.onCorrect: c² − a² under a square root. Rearrange a² + b² = c² to get b² alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Subtracting the lengths doesn't work. The theorem is about squares.
Adding gives a side longer than the hypotenuse. A leg is shorter.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has hypotenuse 25 cm and one leg 7 cm. Find the other leg in centimetres.
hints: The longest side is already known.
Subtract the known leg's square from the hypotenuse's square.
Take the positive square root of 25² − 7².
questions.onCorrect: 24 cm. Subtract the squares, then take the root: 625 − 49 = 576.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the lengths. Subtract the squares, then take the square root.
576 is the square of the missing leg. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has perpendicular legs 9 m and 12 m. Find its hypotenuse in metres.
hints: Use squared lengths before finding the side length.
Add the squares of both legs.
Take the positive square root of 9² + 12².
questions.onCorrect: 15 m. 81 + 144 = 225, and the square root of 225 is 15.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the legs. The theorem adds their squares, then takes the square root.
225 is the square of the hypotenuse. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: How does the shortcut compare with the 7 m path?
hints: Which is shorter: the long way round two sides, or straight across?

acceptedIdeas: The shortcut is shorter than 7 m.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shortcut is the straight line, the shortest route between the two points.

choices.label: The shortcut is shorter than 7 m.
The shortcut is longer than 7 m.

questions.onCorrect: Shorter. A straight line is the shortest route, so it beats the bent path.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 m is the bent path, east then north. A straight line doesn't follow it.
A straight line is the shortest route between two points, so it can't be longer than the bent path.

questions.prompt: Why take the square root at the end?
hints: Is a² + b² a length, or a length squared?

acceptedIdeas: The sum is the square of the hypotenuse, and the root gives its length.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sum is the square of the hypotenuse, and the root gives its length.

choices.label: The sum is the square of the hypotenuse, and the root gives its length.
Because the answer should be smaller.
Because square roots are always whole numbers.

questions.onCorrect: a² + b² gives c × c. The square root undoes the squaring and gives c itself.

misconceptions.feedback: The root does shrink it, but the reason is that the sum is a square of the length.
Many square roots are not whole numbers. The reason is undoing the squaring.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs 8 cm and 15 cm. Find its hypotenuse, in centimetres.
hints: Square each leg.
Add the two squares.
Take the square root of the sum.
questions.onCorrect: 17 cm. 64 + 225 = 289, and the square root of 289 is 17.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the legs. The theorem adds their squares, then takes the square root.
289 is the square of the hypotenuse. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs 20 cm and 21 cm. Find its hypotenuse, in centimetres.
hints: Square each leg.
Add the squares: 400 and 441.
Take the square root of the sum.
questions.onCorrect: 29 cm. 400 + 441 = 841, and the square root of 841 is 29.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the legs. The theorem adds their squares first.
841 is the square of the hypotenuse. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: A 10 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 6 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach, in metres?
hints: The ladder is the hypotenuse. What are the legs?
Subtract the square of the known leg from the square of the ladder.
Take the square root of the difference.
questions.onCorrect: 8 m. The ladder is the hypotenuse, so subtract 36 from 100 and take the root.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the lengths. Subtract the squares, then take the square root.
64 is the square of the height. Take the square root.
